anscombe: Elizabeth Anscombe (1919–2001) was a British analytic philosopher, a student and translator of Wittgenstein. Her 1958 paper 'Modern Moral Philosophy' challenged rule-based ethics and helped revive virtue ethics, and her work on intention made character, weakness of will, and the doctrine of double effect central topics in moral psychology.
bacon: Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was an English philosopher and statesman who argued that science should proceed by systematic observation and experiment rather than inherited authority. In his Novum Organum he catalogued the 'idols' — mental biases — that distort inquiry, and he famously held that knowledge is power over nature.
benjamin: Walter Benjamin (1892–1940) was a German-Jewish cultural critic and philosopher, loosely linked to the Frankfurt School, who blended Marxism with Jewish messianism. His essay 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' argued that mass copies strip artworks of their 'aura', and he wrote influentially on history, cities, and experience.
bourdieu: Pierre Bourdieu (1930–2002) was a French sociologist and philosopher who studied how power reproduces itself invisibly. His concepts of habitus, cultural capital, and field explain why tastes, accents, and manners — not just money — mark class boundaries and let privilege pass quietly from one generation to the next.
buber: Martin Buber (1878–1965) was an Austrian-born Jewish philosopher of religion best known for I and Thou. He distinguished genuine dialogue, in which we meet another person fully as a 'Thou', from the 'I–It' stance that treats people as objects to be used — a distinction that shaped modern philosophy of dialogue and love.
butler: Judith Butler (b. 1956) is an American philosopher and gender theorist whose book Gender Trouble made 'gender performativity' a central idea: gender is not the expression of a natural essence but is constituted, in contested accounts, by repeated stylized acts under social norms. Butler is also a major voice on heteronormativity and vulnerability.
clifford: W. K. Clifford (1845–1879) was a British mathematician and philosopher who argued, in 'The Ethics of Belief', that it is wrong always and everywhere to believe anything on insufficient evidence. His strict evidentialism remains the standard foil in debates about whether faith can be rational.
democritus: Democritus (c. 460–370 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher, sometimes called the 'laughing philosopher', who developed atomism: the view that reality consists of tiny indivisible particles moving in the void. His materialism profoundly influenced Epicurus and, through him, much later scientific thought.
derrida: Jacques Derrida (1930–2004) was an Algerian-born French philosopher, founder of deconstruction and a leading figure of post-structuralism. He argued that texts are built on binary oppositions whose supposedly inferior terms secretly sustain the superior ones, and that reading can expose — never simply escape — these hierarchies.
dubois: W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963) was an American sociologist, historian, and civil-rights leader, the first Black scholar to earn a Harvard doctorate. In The Souls of Black Folk he introduced 'double consciousness': the divided self-awareness of seeing yourself both through your own eyes and through a racist society's.
emerson: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was an American essayist and the leading voice of Transcendentalism, which held that individuals can grasp truth through intuition and nature rather than institutions. His essay 'Self-Reliance', urging nonconformity and trust in one's own mind, deeply shaped American pragmatism and individualism.
fanon: Frantz Fanon (1925–1961) was a Martinican psychiatrist and revolutionary philosopher who analyzed the psychological damage of colonialism. In Black Skin, White Masks and The Wretched of the Earth he examined how racism distorts self-image and recognition, and controversially defended anti-colonial violence as a path to liberation.
frye: Marilyn Frye (b. 1941) is an American feminist philosopher best known for her birdcage metaphor: oppression is not any single barrier but a systematic arrangement of wires that, taken one by one, look easy to step through while together confining a life. Her work analyzes sexism as structural rather than merely personal.
isaiah-berlin: Isaiah Berlin (1909–1997) was a British political philosopher and historian of ideas. His essay 'Two Concepts of Liberty' made the distinction between negative liberty (freedom from interference) and positive liberty (freedom to govern oneself) standard, and he argued for value pluralism: genuine human goods can conflict without error.
leibniz: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was a German rationalist philosopher, mathematician, and polymath who co-invented calculus. He held that reality consists of mind-like simple substances called monads, that nothing happens without a sufficient reason, and that God, being good, created the best of all possible worlds — a claim Voltaire famously mocked.
lyotard: Jean-François Lyotard (1924–1998) was a French philosopher whose The Postmodern Condition defined the postmodern as 'incredulity toward metanarratives' — the grand legitimating stories of progress, emancipation, and science. Drawing on Wittgenstein's language games, he argued knowledge is now plural, local, and contested.
mills: Charles W. Mills (1951–2021) was a Jamaican-born American political philosopher whose The Racial Contract recast the classic social contract: beneath the idealized agreement among equals, he argued, lies an actual contract among whites to rule nonwhites. He championed 'non-ideal theory' against abstract theorizing that ignores race.
paley: William Paley (1743–1805) was an English clergyman and moral philosopher whose watchmaker argument became the classic case for divine design: just as a watch found on a heath implies a watchmaker, the intricate order of nature implies a designer. Darwin knew the argument well and natural selection was posed against it.
parfit: Derek Parfit (1942–2017) was a British philosopher whose Reasons and Persons transformed debates about personal identity. Using thought experiments like the teletransporter, he argued that identity is not what matters for survival; psychological continuity and connectedness are. His later work defended a demanding consequentialist ethics.
rawls: John Rawls (1921–2002) was an American political philosopher whose A Theory of Justice revived political philosophy after decades of dormancy. His 'justice as fairness' asks what principles people would choose behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing their place in society; his difference principle permits inequality only if it benefits the worst off.
reid: Thomas Reid (1710–1796) was a Scottish philosopher, founder of the common-sense school, who answered Hume's skepticism by arguing that trust in perception, memory, and first principles is rational from the start. His objections to Locke's memory theory of personal identity, including the brave-officer case, are still standard in the debate.
russell: Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) was a British philosopher and logician, a founder of analytic philosophy and co-author, with Whitehead, of Principia Mathematica. He worked on logic and the foundations of mathematics, wrote famously clear essays on skepticism, religion, and the meaning of life, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
sextus-empiricus: Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 AD) was a Greek physician and Pyrrhonian skeptic whose surviving books are our main record of ancient skepticism. He argued that for every claim an equal counter-claim can be raised, so wisdom lies in suspending judgment — a stance that reshaped modern philosophy when rediscovered in the Renaissance.
spinoza: Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was a Dutch philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish origin, excommunicated from his community, who built a rigorous rationalist system. He held that there is only one infinite substance — God, or Nature — that everything follows with necessity, and that freedom comes from understanding necessity rather than escaping it.
